Which is not to say that TIPS will generate a positive return over the next 5 years. But they should outperform nominals if inflation stays elevated, and no worse than nominals if inflation reverts to 2.5%. 🧵(7/7)

My conclusion? Today, at a 5-year break-even of 2.35%, a real 5-year yield of 2.62%, and a nominal 5-year yield of 5.0%, the choice is to buy the nominal Treasuries at attractive yields but run the risk that inflation is more than 2.35% over the next five years. Or, I can buy 5yr TIPS and lock in that juicy 2.62% real yield but without knowing whether the realized inflation component will be big enough to compete with nominals. Based on my simple exercise and my expectation that the old 2% inflation regime is past and that the 3-4% regime of the last 5 years is here to stay, my clear choice is TIPS with their compelling real yield and (too) low breakeven. 🧵 (6/7)

TIPS or nominals? With apologies to my fixed income colleagues for assessing this important asset class in such a rudimentary and primitive way (and ignoring what I am sure are a myriad of nuances), my conclusion is as follows. TIPS will outperform nominals (if held to maturity) if the realized forward CPI exceeds the current break-even, and vice versa. Duh. Can it really be that simple? Probably not, but bear with me. 🧵(1/7)

Inflationary pressures are intensifying in the US manufacturing sector:

The ISM Manufacturing Prices Paid Index surged +6.8 points in September, to 77.9, its highest since May.

This also marks its largest monthly increase since February.

Year-to-date, the index has soared +19.4 points, its third-biggest 9-month increase since 2021.

Meanwhile, the ISM Manufacturing PMI index eased slightly in September by -0.1 point, to 54.5, remaining in expansion for the 9th consecutive month, its longest streak since 2022.

Furthermore, new orders rose +1.6 points, to 55.3, also posting their 9th consecutive monthly expansion.

And, the backlog of unfilled orders jumped +4.6 points, to 56.4, its 2nd-highest level since May 2022.

Manufacturing price pressures are building as elevated demand puts further strain on capacity.

An important question is what to put in the bond bucket in the 60/20/20. Nominals or TIPS? I have been struggling with the question of whether TIPS are better than nominal bonds in this rising rate regime. They have been so far this year, but not by much (-1.7% vs -2.3% for the Agg). I have been exploring the relative value question for some time and only managed to confuse myself with the myriads of variables to consider. Are they real assets or bonds, or both? When do they behave like bonds and when do the behave like real assets? Are they driven by real yields or by break-evens? We see from the scatterplot below that the direction of travel for nominal and real yields is correlated (0.89 R-squared), but it’s not clear from the chart when and why TIPS might outperform (the size of the dots). 🧵(1/2)

Anyone following my sentiment work knows I’ve been contrarian-bullish about Bitcoin’s price for most of the summer.

Today I want to show you why.

And it’s not because of my loosely held opinion or market intuition, but because of the raw data I’ve been immersed in.

It’s this data that’s led me to be so confidently bullish at precisely the time people have been crashing out about Bitcoin, screaming about oil, and rotating into AI stocks. Today I’m going to show you exactly what I was looking at back then so you can better understand it yourself.

And to start off, I’ve got some bad news.

The Fear & Greed Index sucks.

I know, I know, it hurts to hear.

People have latched onto the idea that these two emotions somehow drive the entire market, but it misses the nuance. Humans’ relationship with markets is far more nuanced than good/bad, bullish/bearish, or fear/greed.

So today we’ll explore some of that nuance.

First, we’ll focus on excitement.

And (like every indicator we’ll look at today) this is contrarian.

When every single bitcoiner is excited about what’s on the horizon, it can often be a riskier time to buy bitcoin. I’ve shared this data in a variety of ways, but I’ve got a brand-new one for you today that I think makes it clearer than ever why I have been so consistently bullish over the last few months.

This lets us visualize when excitement is historically elevated or depressed.

A red dot indicates excitement is in the top 20% historically, and a green dot indicates excitement is in the bottom 20%.

There are multiple ways to look at it, but the simplest is that a red dot indicates a slightly riskier time to enter a Bitcoin position than a green dot, which represents a de-risked time to enter a Bitcoin position from an excitement perspective.

“Cool dots bro, but like how does this actually perform?”

Glad you asked.

Bitcoin price 6 months later:

• Bottom 20% excitement: +42.3%
• Top 20% excitement: +10.2%

Bitcoin price 2 years later:

• Bottom 20% excitement: +192.4%
• Top 20% excitement: -2.2%

An astute reader may have already noticed a consistent chain of green dots through most of the summer… a chain only rivaled by the boredom and apathy of most of 2020 before the 2021 euphoria.

That's precisely why I’ve been so bullish.

It’s not just that moods have been low.

It’s that they’ve been historically low for an extended period.

“Ya, but this is just excitement language. You’re really going to base your entire market thesis around the words people are using?”

1) Language contains way more signal than most people realize.

2) We aren’t just analyzing words… but investigating crowd psychology.

3) I’m only just scratching the surface.

Let’s go a bit deeper.
